claim: Lees-Shepard et al. reported that palovarotene (a retinoid agonist) had severe side effects on growth plate and limb joints in an Acvr1R206H knock-in mouse model of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP).
source: Lees-Shepard et al. reported that palovarotene (a retinoid agonist) had severe side effects on growth plate and limb joints in an Acvr1R206H knock-in mouse model of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the Lees-Shepard et al. 2018 study.

claim: Lees-Shepard et al. used a retinoid drug delivery method that is never used in the treatment of patients.
source: Lees-Shepard et al. write that "it is important for FOP therapeutics to exhibit an acceptable safety profile in juvenile patients": however, they used a retinoid drug delivery method that is never used in the treatment of patients, thus undermining their goal.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their knowledge of clinical practice and the methods used in the Lees-Shepard study.

claim: The mouse model used by Lees-Shepard et al. does not sufficiently mimic FOP patients.
source: Moreover, the mouse model used does not sufficiently mimic FOP patients.
evidence: This is an evaluative claim made by the authors based on their analysis of the mouse model characteristics compared to FOP patient characteristics.

claim: Palovarotene was originally designed for oral administration.
source: Palovarotene was originally designed for oral administration (Hind and Stinchcombe, 2009), allowing for low and steady drug adsorption by the digestive system and an overall absorption efficiency of 50% to 65% of administered dose, typical of retinoids (Blaner and Olson, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hind and Stinchcombe, 2009.

claim: Oral administration of palovarotene allows for low and steady drug adsorption by the digestive system.
source: Palovarotene was originally designed for oral administration (Hind and Stinchcombe, 2009), allowing for low and steady drug adsorption by the digestive system and an overall absorption efficiency of 50% to 65% of administered dose, typical of retinoids (Blaner and Olson, 1994).
evidence: This claim is based on the cited reference about palovarotene's design and general knowledge about oral drug administration.

claim: Oral administration of palovarotene results in an overall absorption efficiency of 50% to 65% of administered dose, typical of retinoids.
source: Palovarotene was originally designed for oral administration (Hind and Stinchcombe, 2009), allowing for low and steady drug adsorption by the digestive system and an overall absorption efficiency of 50% to 65% of administered dose, typical of retinoids (Blaner and Olson, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blaner and Olson, 1994, regarding retinoid absorption efficiency.

claim: Lees-Shepard et al. injected palovarotene intraperitoneally (IP) every day for 4 weeks.
source: Instead, Lees-Shepard et al. injected the drug intraperitoneally (IP) every day for 4 weeks.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the methods used in the Lees-Shepard et al. study.

claim: The IP route of administration is known to invariably cause a sharp and sudden increase in circulating drug levels, resulting in a higher and faster Cmax compared to oral delivery.
source: This IP route of administration is known to invariably cause a sharp and sudden increase in circulating drug levels, resulting in a higher and faster Cmax compared to oral delivery (Eaton and Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eaton and Gilbert, 2013.

claim: Palovarotene Cmax levels were found to be about 6-fold higher after IP injection compared to oral administration in mice.
source: Indeed, palovarotene Cmax levels were found to be about 6-fold higher after IP injection compared to oral administration in mice (Clementia Pharmaceuticals, internal data).
evidence: This claim is supported by internal data from Clementia Pharmaceuticals.

claim: Circulating retinoids are quickly taken up by tissues and cells.
source: Circulating retinoids are quickly taken up by tissues and cells (Cullum and Zile, 1985), and cells accumulate retinoids in large amounts intracellularly (Kurlandsky et al., 1995; Randolph and Simon, 1997) where their action on cell function and phenotype can last hours to days (Chen and Gudas, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cullum and Zile, 1985.

claim: Cells accumulate retinoids in large amounts intracellularly.
source: Circulating retinoids are quickly taken up by tissues and cells (Cullum and Zile, 1985), and cells accumulate retinoids in large amounts intracellularly (Kurlandsky et al., 1995; Randolph and Simon, 1997) where their action on cell function and phenotype can last hours to days (Chen and Gudas, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kurlandsky et al., 1995 and Randolph and Simon, 1997.

claim: Retinoid action on cell function and phenotype can last hours to days.
source: Circulating retinoids are quickly taken up by tissues and cells (Cullum and Zile, 1985), and cells accumulate retinoids in large amounts intracellularly (Kurlandsky et al., 1995; Randolph and Simon, 1997) where their action on cell function and phenotype can last hours to days (Chen and Gudas, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen and Gudas, 1996.

claim: Daily IP injections are expected to result in ever increasing and possibly confounding drug effects over time.
source: Thus, daily IP injections are expected to result in ever increasing and possibly confounding drug effects over time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the previously cited information about retinoid uptake, accumulation, and duration of action.

claim: Lees-Shepard et al. stated that they used palovarotene doses that correspond to approximate adult human equivalent doses of 3.6 mg and 7.2 mg.
source: Lees-Shepard et al. stated that they used "palovarotene doses….that correspond to approximate adult human equivalent doses of 3.6 mg and 7.2 mg" under testing in ongoing efficacy and safety study of palovarotene for the treatment of FOP being conducted by Clementia Pharmaceuticals (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03312634. This trial has recently entered phase 3).
evidence: This is a statement about what Lees-Shepard et al. reported in their study, with reference to a clinical trial.

claim: The IP administration changed the effective dose and undermined the goal of testing a clinically relevant treatment.
source: However, the IP administration changed the effective dose and undermined the goal of testing a clinically relevant treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the previously discussed differences between IP and oral administration.

claim: Lees-Shepard et al. utilized a conditional mouse model in which the FOP causative gene was activated in Pdgfrα-expressing cells by mating floxed Acvr1R206H mice with Pdgfrα-Cre mice.
source: Lees-Shepard et al. utilized a conditional mouse model in which the FOP causative gene was activated in Pdgfrα-expressing cells by mating floxed Acvr1R206H mice with Pdgfrα-Cre mice.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the mouse model used in the Lees-Shepard et al. study.

claim: Pdgfrα-expressing cells were described as a subpopulation of progenitor cells particularly sensitive to effects of the mutation.
source: Those cells were described as a subpopulation of progenitor cells particularly sensitive to effects of the mutation.
evidence: This is a statement about how the cells were characterized in the Lees-Shepard et al. study.

claim: The Pdgfrα-Cre mouse model is at sharp variance with FOP patients in which the mutant ACVR1R206H gene characterizes the majority of, if not all, cells.
source: This mouse model is at sharp variance with FOP patients in which the mutant ACVR1R206H gene characterizes the majority of, if not all, cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of FOP genetics and comparison with the mouse model.

claim: Data obtained with the Pdgfrα-Cre mouse model may be skewed by targeting a specific subpopulation of cells that could also be affected by wild-type cells.
source: Thus, data obtained with the Pdgfrα-Cre mouse model may be skewed by targeting a specific subpopulation of cells that could also be affected by wild-type cells, with the wild-type cells likely outnumbering the cells in the specific Acvr1R206H subpopulation and interacting with them.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential confounding factors in the mouse model.

claim: Wild-type cells likely outnumber the cells in the specific Acvr1R206H subpopulation and interact with them in the Pdgfrα-Cre mouse model.
source: Thus, data obtained with the Pdgfrα-Cre mouse model may be skewed by targeting a specific subpopulation of cells that could also be affected by wild-type cells, with the wild-type cells likely outnumbering the cells in the specific Acvr1R206H subpopulation and interacting with them.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conditional nature of the mouse model.

claim: The Pdgfrα-Cre mouse model does not faithfully reproduce the overall genetic makeup and cell and tissue responses in FOP patients.
source: Thus, the model does not faithfully reproduce the overall genetic makeup and cell and tissue responses in FOP patients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between the mouse model and FOP patient genetics.

claim: Lees-Shepard et al. observed that Pdgfrα+ cells contributed to heterotopic ossification (HO) in their model.
source: While Lees-Shepard et al. observed that Pdgfrα+ cells contributed to heterotopic ossification (HO) in their model, it is not known whether this specific cell population is clinically relevant in FOP patients.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from the Lees-Shepard et al. study.

claim: It is not known whether Pdgfrα+ cells are clinically relevant in FOP patients.
source: While Lees-Shepard et al. observed that Pdgfrα+ cells contributed to heterotopic ossification (HO) in their model, it is not known whether this specific cell population is clinically relevant in FOP patients.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of knowledge regarding the clinical relevance of this cell population.

claim: Lees-Shepard et al. presented no data showing that targeted Pdgfrα+ cells were present in the growing skeleton.
source: Further, Lees-Shepard et al. presented no data showing that targeted Pdgfrα+ cells were present in the growing skeleton.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of specific data in the Lees-Shepard et al. study.

claim: The Pdgfrα gene is not known to be expressed in chondrocytes.
source: Given that the Pdgfrα gene is not known to be expressed in chondrocytes (Hamilton et al., 2003), it is nearly certain that growth plate and articular chondrocytes were not targeted by Pdgfrα-Cre and remained largely, if not totally, wild-type.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hamilton et al., 2003.

claim: It is nearly certain that growth plate and articular chondrocytes were not targeted by Pdgfrα-Cre and remained largely, if not totally, wild-type.
source: Given that the Pdgfrα gene is not known to be expressed in chondrocytes (Hamilton et al., 2003), it is nearly certain that growth plate and articular chondrocytes were not targeted by Pdgfrα-Cre and remained largely, if not totally, wild-type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of Pdgfrα expression in chondrocytes.

claim: Lees-Shepard et al. included no data to demonstrate that Pdgfrα-Cre had targeted growth plate and joint chondrocytes.
source: Lees-Shepard et al. included no data to demonstrate that Pdgfrα-Cre had targeted growth plate and joint chondrocytes.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of specific data in the Lees-Shepard et al. study.

claim: Studies dating back decades have established that cartilage is sensitive to systemic retinoid levels.
source: Studies dating back decades have established that cartilage is sensitive to systemic retinoid levels (Wolbach and Hegsted, 1953).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wolbach and Hegsted, 1953.

claim: The authors observed a slight growth retardation of about 10% in control wild type mice after oral palovarotene administration.
source: In our studies (Chakkalakal et al., 2016; Shimono et al., 2011), we did observe a slight growth retardation of about 10% in control wild type mice after oral palovarotene administration, although their growth plates remained open and there were no obvious effects on their joints.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' own studies, cited as Chakkalakal et al., 2016 and Shimono et al., 2011.

claim: Growth plates remained open in control wild type mice after oral palovarotene administration.
source: In our studies (Chakkalakal et al., 2016; Shimono et al., 2011), we did observe a slight growth retardation of about 10% in control wild type mice after oral palovarotene administration, although their growth plates remained open and there were no obvious effects on their joints.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' own studies.

claim: There were no obvious effects on joints in control wild type mice after oral palovarotene administration.
source: In our studies (Chakkalakal et al., 2016; Shimono et al., 2011), we did observe a slight growth retardation of about 10% in control wild type mice after oral palovarotene administration, although their growth plates remained open and there were no obvious effects on their joints.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' own studies.

claim: There were no obvious growth retardation and growth plate effects after oral palovarotene administration in Prrx1-Cre; Acvr1R206H mutant mice in which the entire limb mesenchymal cell population was targeted, including skeletal cells.
source: Notably, there were no obvious growth retardation and growth plate effects after oral palovarotene administration in our Prrx1-Cre; Acvr1R206H mutant mice in which the entire limb mesenchymal cell population was targeted, including skeletal cells.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the authors' own studies with a different mouse model.

claim: The higher tolerance of mutant growth plates was likely due to higher basal levels of canonical BMP signaling activity.
source: The higher tolerance of mutant growth plates was likely due to higher basal levels of canonical BMP signaling activity.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the observed tolerance.

claim: Palovarotene may be quite safe for – and well tolerated by – FOP patients.
source: As we pointed out previously (Chakkalakal et al., 2016), this provides support to the notion that palovarotene may be quite safe for – and well tolerated by – FOP patients, as supported by the announcement of Phase 2 Part B data from the ongoing efficacy and safety study being conducted by Clementia (Clementia Pharmaceuticals, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by inference from the authors' data and citation to clinical trial results.

claim: The severe side effects on growth plates and joints observed by Lees-Shepard et al. are likely the results of the route of drug administration, excessive palovarotene levels and effects likely caused by the daily IP administration, and reliance on a mouse model that does not mimic FOP patients, including apparent lack of mutation expression in cartilage.
source: In sum, the severe side effects on growth plates and joints observed by Lees-Shepard et al. are likely the results of: (i) the route of drug administration; (ii) excessive palovarotene levels and effects likely caused by the daily IP administration; and (iii) reliance on a mouse model that does not mimic FOP patients, including apparent lack of mutation expression in cartilage.
evidence: This is an inference and conclusion drawn from the authors' analysis of the Lees-Shepard et al. study.
